sections.html:
Martinsburg is the seat of Berkeley County, which fills 321.56 square miles of the Shenandoah Valley in West Virginia's Eastern Panhandle. It forms part of the Hagerstown-Martinsburg metropolitan area, and only Kanawha County has more people among the state's 55 counties.

The county had 122,076 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 139,522 is about 14 percent higher. More people usually means more buyers, but it also means new homes on the market that compete with an older one. Six magisterial districts make up the county: Adam Stephens, Norborne, Potomac, Shenandoah, Tuscarora and Valley.

A few local numbers are worth saving before you list:

  • Berkeley County Commission: 400 W. Stephen St., Martinsburg, 304-264-1923.
  • City of Martinsburg: 232 N. Queen St., 304-264-2131.
  • Sheriff's Tax Office: (304) 264-1982, for balances.
  • County Assessor: 304-264-1904.
  • Eastern Panhandle Organization of Homeowners Associations: 304-728-2201.
  • West Virginia State Tax Department: 800-982-8297.

Is your house in a homeowners association? Get a written statement of unpaid dues before closing, because the title company and the buyer will ask whether anything is owed. An older house may also carry a local historic designation. Check with the city or county first if you are thinking about exterior work or tearing the house down.

The assessor in your county decides value, and the sheriff handles bills and collection. Each July 1 freezes the picture of a parcel, meaning its owner, its use and its worth, for the calendar tax year that follows. Property tax is levied by county boards of education, county commissions, municipalities and the State.

Parcels are sorted by the constitution into four classes:

  • Class I: intangibles and some farm personal property, currently untaxed.
  • Class II: the owner's own residence used for nothing else, plus farmland in agricultural use.
  • Class III: remaining property located outside any municipality.
  • Class IV: remaining property located inside a municipality.

Suppose an investor buys your house and rents it out. The house leaves Class II, and the tax can shift after the sale.

The county commission hears protests while acting as the board of equalization and review. It starts on February 1 and wraps up by February 28, and you need to file before that year's taxes fall due. To prepare:

  • Line up evidence of value, such as an independent appraisal or repair estimates.
  • Look for errors in the assessor's record on square footage, bedrooms or condition.
  • Call the assessor's office to learn how to file with the commission at 400 West Stephen Street, Suite 106, Martinsburg.
  • A dispute about classification or taxability can be sent to the Tax Commissioner under West Virginia Code 11-3-24a, and a ruling is due by the end of February.

The state sends a notice when an assessed value rises. A higher number changes what the buyer will owe, so read yours before closing.

The sheriff issues tickets from July 15 onward. You owe half on September 1 and half on March 1, with a discount for paying before each date. Interest begins once a half is delinquent, on October 1 for the first and April 1 for the second.

December 1 is the last day to apply for the homestead exemption. West Virginia Code 11-6B-3 exempts $20,000 of assessed value, the first slice, for an owner who is 65 or older or certified permanently and totally disabled, and who lived in West Virginia for the two consecutive calendar years before the tax year. Drawing a similar exemption in another state disqualifies you here.

For a balance, phone the Sheriff's Tax Office at (304) 264-1982. The County Assessor's number is 304-264-1904. Confirm any date with the office before you rely on it.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Berkeley County
sections.html:
With no buyer's mortgage, the usual West Virginia closing gets simpler. Describe the house to us, read the written offer that comes back, and make your call. Then an attorney or title company files the deed, pays liens and takes care of tax.

Houses are bought as-is by Cash Home Buyers. The seller pays no fees, commissions or closing costs, and declining costs nothing.

• Heirs in different states sharing an inherited house.
  • An HOA property with dues unpaid.
  • A rental the landlord is tired of managing.
  • A tax installment that is behind, with interest building.

Each has an obvious first move. With an HOA, ask for the balance in writing. With taxes, ask the Sheriff's Tax Office for the figure. With an inherited house, collect the death certificate and the court papers. This page gives general information and is not legal or tax advice, so verify specifics with the county office or a qualified professional.

sections.h2: Timeline for listing or selling for cash
sections.html:
Start with the tax side, because it affects every other step. Get the balance and the half it applies to. Next, ask for the HOA statement if there is one, and request any papers an heir needs. Then decide whether a listing or a cash sale fits your schedule. A listing depends on showings and on a buyer's financing, so expect inspection requests and a wait for the buyer's lender. A cash sale depends on title work and on the closing date you choose.

Whichever route you take, keep the order straight on closing day: the title company settles liens and taxes first, and what remains is yours. If the second installment on March 1 or the first on September 1 is close, ask how it will be divided between you and the buyer. Keep the tax ticket and the assessor's notice together in one folder, because the title company may ask for either.

Martinsburg sellers who are weighing the two routes can compare them on the table above: a listing brings commission and seller closing costs, and a cash sale does not. Spend an afternoon on the phone first. One call to the Sheriff's Tax Office, one to the assessor and one to your HOA, if you have one, will tell you most of what a buyer or title company is going to ask. Write down each answer with the date, so the closing agent can see where every figure came from.

faqs.q: Until when can I protest my assessment?
faqs.a: Until the board of equalization and review adjourns, no later than February 28. It begins sitting February 1, and your protest must come before that year's taxes are due.

faqs.q: What are the two payment dates?
faqs.a: September 1 for the first half and March 1 for the second, after tickets are issued from July 15. The halves turn delinquent on October 1 and April 1.
Someone who owns and lives in the home, is 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled, and has two years of West Virginia residency. The application is due December 1.

faqs.q: Does the bill change if my buyer rents the house?
faqs.a: Yes, it can. Class II belongs to a house the owner lives in, and a rental drops into Class III or Class IV, depending on whether the property is inside a municipality.

faqs.q: What does a cash sale to Cash Home Buyers cost?
faqs.a: No fees at all. The purchase is as-is, with no commissions or closing costs charged to you, and saying no to the offer costs nothing.
